turns.content: I’m starting a three-year contract soon—two weeks at a mine in northern Nevada, then two weeks back in Denver. I just ended a four-year relationship because my ex wanted me to quit fieldwork for a desk job. I’m not doing that again. So I need a concrete plan for dating during my off-weeks. How do I schedule this efficiently and filter for someone who won’t resent the travel?

**Basis:** Your rotation is fixed (14 on / 14 off), so the plan below treats it as the constraint and works backward from what is observable in a prospective partner. Research on fly-in/fly-out (FIFO) workers—mostly Australian mining—finds even-time rosters like 2/2 are associated with better partner satisfaction than longer-away rosters, and that roster predictability and contact quality during absence matter more than absence itself (e.g., Gardner et al. 2018; WA Parliament FIFO inquiry 2015). Effect sizes are modest and the samples are mostly married couples, so this transfers only partly to early dating.

## Scheduling

**Calendar structure per 28-day cycle**
- Off-block day 1: no dates. Travel day plus adjustment; FIFO studies consistently flag the first 24–48 h home as the highest-friction window.
- Off-block days 2–5: front-load first dates (2–4). This leaves days 6–13 for second/third dates with the same person inside one block.
- Off-block day 14: no dates; pack, prep.
- On-block: messaging and voice/video only. Confirm cell/Wi-Fi availability at the site before you promise contact frequency—many Nevada sites have limited coverage in camp, and 12-hour shifts leave roughly 2–3 usable hours/day.

**Arithmetic to set expectations:** you get ~10 usable dating days per 28. Reaching the point most people reach after ~3 months of conventional dating will take you ~6 months. Plan for that; do not compress it by over-scheduling.

**App logistics**
- Set location to Denver. Put the roster in the first line of the profile: "2 weeks at a mine in NV / 2 weeks in Denver, fixed schedule through [year]."
- Match and message during on-weeks; only propose meeting with a specific date inside your next off-block. This filters out people who need to meet within 72 hours and gives you a queue for days 2–5.
- Limit to one or two apps; you don't have bandwidth for more.

## Filtering

Stating the constraint up front removes people who self-select out. It does not identify who will be fine with it long-term—people are poor at predicting how they'll feel about absence before experiencing it. So use two layers.

**Layer 1 — early screen (first two dates).** Look for observable facts, not stated attitudes:
- They have an existing life that runs without a partner: standing commitments, friends they see weekly, a job with its own demands.
- Prior exposure to a comparable schedule: dated or grew up with military, oilfield, nursing, travel-heavy, or academic-field partners. Ask what worked and what didn't.
- When you describe the roster, they ask logistical questions ("what's contact like out there?") rather than "would you ever change that?" The second question is not disqualifying by itself, but note it.
- Their answer to: "If we were together in a year and I missed something that mattered to you because I was on shift, how do you think you'd handle it?" You're listening for a concrete answer, not reassurance.

**Layer 2 — behavioral test (cycles 1–3 of dating someone).** This is the only reliable filter.
- Contact during on-weeks is steady and not a source of friction about frequency.
- Reunions don't produce a recurring argument about the schedule within the first 48 h.
- They make plans for their own on-weeks rather than waiting.
- By cycle 3 (~3 months), you can ask directly whether the schedule is costing them something and get a specific answer.

If any of these fails in two consecutive cycles, the pattern is more informative than any prior statement.

## Two cautions
- Your prior relationship is one data point about one person's preferences. It does not tell you the base rate of people who accept a 2/2 roster, which is unknown but nonzero—FIFO workers do maintain long-term relationships at rates broadly comparable to the general population in the studies above.
- Don't advertise the roster as something they must "accept." Present it as a fixed fact, then evaluate behavior. People who would be fine with it are still put off by a framing that reads as pre-emptive defense.

**Next action:** before your first rotation, confirm site connectivity and shift length, then write the two-line profile with the roster in line one and set your first off-block's days 2–5 as your dating window.

I appreciate the research citations—that's the kind of specificity I like. But eight to ten first dates per 14-day off-block is the target, not negotiable. I can sleep when I'm old. What I need is a system for that volume: app sequencing, time-blocked coffee slots, and a rubric for filtering on logistics before chemistry.

**Basis:** Ten first dates in 12 usable days is arithmetically feasible at ~1/day with two double-days. The design constraint is not time; it is funnel attrition and decision quality at volume. Speed-dating research (Lenton & Francesconi 2010, n≈3,700 daters) found that when the number of options per session rose from ~15–20 to ~30+, participants shifted toward easily observed traits (height, weight, age) and made fewer selections. The system below moves all logistics screening off the date so the 45 minutes is spent only on what messaging can't assess.

## Funnel arithmetic (assumptions marked)

Target: 10 first dates confirmed and attended per off-block.
- Cancellation/no-show rate for app first dates: assume 25–35% (industry-reported, not peer-reviewed; track your own rate after block 1).
- Therefore schedule 13–14 dates.
- Conversations that reach a scheduled date: assume 40–50%. Need ~28–35 active conversations.
- Matches that become conversations: assume ~50%. Need ~60–70 matches per 28 days.

Revise all four numbers with your own data after the first cycle. Two cycles of tracking gives you a personal conversion table that replaces these assumptions.

## App sequencing across the 28-day cycle

**On-block days 1–7:** Open new matches only. Run two apps (Hinge for prompt-based screening; one swipe-based app for volume). Do not schedule yet—matches older than 10 days at first-meet have higher drop-off (unverified; check your own data).

**On-block days 8–12:** Screen via message using the rubric below. Move survivors to "propose date." Send specific slot offers: "I'm back in Denver the [date]. Coffee [day] 10:00 or [day] 14:00 at [venue]?" Two options only.

**On-block days 13–14:** Lock 13–14 slots. Send a one-line confirmation the day before each.

**Off-block:** No new matching days 1–10; that time is spent on dates. Days 11–14: reopen matching for the next cycle so the pipeline is warm when you fly out.

## Time-blocked slot template (off-block)

Fixed venue within 10 minutes of your home. Fixed duration: 45 minutes, stated in the invite ("I've got 45 before the next thing"). This is normal for coffee dates and removes the awkward exit.

| Day | 10:00 | 14:00 | 18:30 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | — | — | — |
| 2 | 1st | 1st | — |
| 3 | 1st | — | — |
| 4 | 1st | 1st | — |
| 5 | 1st | — | — |
| 6 | 1st | 1st | — |
| 7 | 1st | — | 2nd |
| 8 | 1st | — | 2nd |
| 9 | (1st, backup) | — | 2nd |
| 10 | (1st, backup) | — | 2nd/3rd |
| 11 | — | — | 3rd |
| 12 | — | — | 3rd |
| 13 | — | — | open |
| 14 | — | — | — |

- 10 primary first-date slots days 2–8, 2–4 backup slots days 9–10 for reschedules.
- Evenings days 7–12 reserved for second/third dates with the 2–3 people who cleared the first date. If you fill those evenings with additional first dates, you exit the block with no second dates and restart from zero each cycle.
- Never three first dates in one day. Speed-dating data show recall and discrimination degrade after ~8 sequential encounters in a session; two per day with a 4-hour gap is the ceiling I would use.

## Rubric: logistics before chemistry

**Stage A — Profile/first messages (pass/fail, before proposing a date).** Fail on any:
1. Lives >25 minutes from your Denver base. At 10 usable days/month you can't absorb commute.
2. Cannot do weekday daytime dates. Your off-block includes 10 weekdays; a partner locked to weekend-only availability shrinks your overlap to ~4 days/cycle.
3. States or implies a relocation plan within 3 years incompatible with a Denver base.
4. Profile or messages indicate needing daily in-person contact ("hate long distance," "need someone around").
5. Asks to meet during your on-block after you've stated the roster (indicates they didn't register it).

**Stage B — Pre-date message screen (score 0–2 each, need ≥6/10 to book).**
1. Response latency stable rather than bursty (proxy for how on-week texting will go).
2. Their own schedule has fixed structure (shift work, travel, demanding job, or heavy standing commitments).
3. Asks a logistics question about the roster (connectivity, roster length, contract end).
4. Prior exposure to rotation/travel partners, stated or inferable.
5. Agrees to a specific slot on first offer without renegotiating venue/time (proxy for low-friction planning).

**Stage C — The 45 minutes (chemistry only).** Two questions, asked the same way every time so results are comparable:
- "What does a normal Tuesday look like for you?" You're listening for a life that runs on its own.
- "Last time a plan fell through on you—what happened?" You're listening for a concrete story, not a judgment of the other person.
Score 0–2 on each, plus 0–2 on whether you'd want a second 45 minutes. Second date at ≥4/6.

**Stage D — Post-date (48 h).** They respond to your follow-up within a day; they don't renegotiate the roster ("so would you ever…"). Fail either → no second date.

## Tracking

One spreadsheet row per match: source app, days from match to date, rubric scores A–D, outcome. After block 2 you'll have ~20 rows; after block 4, ~40. That is enough to see which Stage B items predict passing Stage D, and to drop the ones that don't.

## Tradeoff stated once

At this volume, your funnel will select for people who are good at fast logistics and available on short notice. That overlaps with, but is not identical to, people who tolerate a 2/2 roster over three years. Stage D and the behavioral test from my prior message (cycles 1–3 with one person) are where that gets tested; the coffee slots don't measure it.

**Next action:** build the spreadsheet and the Stage A/B checklist before your first on-block, and set your fixed venue and the three slot times now so every invite is copy-paste.

The spreadsheet template is workable, actually. But I’m stuck on the disclosure timing. Do I put the rotation in my profile or wait until we’ve met? Because if I lead with it, I filter hard and fast, but I also broadcast my exact vulnerability to every stranger. And if I wait, I’ve wasted a 45-minute slot on someone who’ll walk when they hear it.

**Basis:** Your own system already answers this—Stage A item 5 and Stage B item 3 both require the roster to be known before booking. The remaining question is resolution: how much detail, at which stage. The answer is to disclose the fact early and the specifics late.

## Recommendation: three-tier disclosure

**Tier 1 — Profile (fact only).**
"2 weeks on / 2 weeks off. Denver-based, fixed schedule, multi-year contract."
Include: the rotation pattern, that it's fixed, that Denver is home.
Exclude: employer, site name, state, contract dates, flight days, neighborhood.

**Tier 2 — Pre-booking message (confirmation).**
One line before proposing slots: "Heads up since some people skim profiles—I'm away half of every month for work. Still up for coffee?" This catches non-readers (Stage A #5) and gives you the logistics-question signal (Stage B #3) before you spend a slot.

**Tier 3 — After a second date, at your discretion (specifics).**
Where the site is, when your next block starts, your address. Nobody who has not cleared Stage D needs to know which 14 days your home is empty.

## Why not wait until after meeting

- Cost of waiting: some fraction of first dates will end on the roster alone. That fraction is unknown; if it is 30–50%, you burn 3–5 of 10 slots per block on people who would have filtered themselves out for free. Any nonzero fraction makes waiting the more expensive option at your volume.
- Online-dating self-disclosure research (Gibbs, Ellison & Heino 2006, n=349) finds that people who anticipate meeting in person disclose more honestly and earlier, and that disclosure of constraints before meeting is associated with higher rated success of the resulting date. Effect sizes are modest and the sample is one U.S. dating site, but the direction is consistent.
- Withholding a fixed structural fact until after meeting reads to many people as a managed reveal. That frame costs you with exactly the low-friction, straightforward people your Stage B rubric is selecting for.

## On "broadcasting vulnerability"

Separate two things you've combined:

1. **Physical/security exposure.** Real, but it attaches to specifics (address + dates), not to the fact of a rotation. A profile saying "away half of each month" tells a stranger nothing actionable. The Tier 3 rule handles this. Standard first-date practice (public venue, they don't know where you live) already covers the rest.

2. **Being filtered on the roster.** This is the point of the profile line, not a cost. You've defined a person who declines on the roster as outside your target. Their declining early is the filter working.

If "vulnerability" means something else—the roster being the thing your last relationship ended over—that is a report about your history, not a property of the disclosure. The people reading your profile do not have that history.

## What this does to the funnel

Profile disclosure lowers match volume by an unknown amount. Compensate by raising top-of-funnel activity in on-block days 1–7 rather than by softening the line. Track match rate for two blocks; if it is under the ~60–70 you need, widen distance radius or add a third app before removing the disclosure.

**Next action:** write the Tier 1 line and the Tier 2 message now, save both as copy-paste text, and add a "roster acknowledged Y/N" column to the spreadsheet so you can measure whether Tier 2 actually reduces on-date walkouts.

I hear you on the security exposure versus filtering tradeoff. The three-tier structure is sensible. But I keep circling back to the same knot: the rotation is exactly what ended my last relationship. Putting it in a profile feels like leading with the wound, even if strangers can't see the history.

**Basis:** Nothing in this turn changes the disclosure analysis; the three-tier structure stands. What's left is the frame you're applying to Tier 1, and the frame doesn't match the facts you've reported.

## What the record shows

- The rotation did not end the relationship. Your partner asked you to give it up; you declined and ended it. That is a choice you made, twice—once in the breakup, once in signing a three-year contract. The profile line states that choice.
- A wound is something done to you. A constraint you selected and are keeping is a fact about your life, in the same category as "I have a kid" or "I don't drink." People put those in profiles as a matter of course.
- One relationship ending over the roster is one data point about one person. It tells you nothing about how the next 60 people who read the line will react, and it gives the line no meaning they can detect.

## What "leading with the wound" would actually look like

Compare:
- "2 weeks on / 2 weeks off. Denver-based, fixed schedule." — a fact.
- "I travel for work and I'm not changing that for anyone." — a defense.

The first is Tier 1. The second is the wound. My caution in the first message was about this exact distinction: present the roster as a fixed fact, not as something they must accept. If your draft line reads like the second, rewrite it. If it reads like the first, the discomfort is yours, not the line's.

## Two observations, not conclusions

1. You reported the knot as recurring ("keep circling back"). I can note that; I can't tell you what it means. If it persists across the first two off-blocks and shows up on dates—as pre-emptive explaining, or as bristling when someone asks a normal logistics question—that is observable, and it will cost you with the low-friction people your rubric selects for. Watch for it and log it in the spreadsheet alongside Stage D.
2. The breakup is recent. The volume plan does not depend on the knot being resolved first, but the knot is more likely to leak into Stage C at 10 dates per block than at 3. That is a tradeoff you've already accepted; I'm naming where it will show.

**Next action:** write the Tier 1 line, then read it aloud once as if it were someone else's profile. If it sounds like a fact, ship it. If it sounds like an argument, cut words until it doesn't.

You’re right that the framing matters—I can see the distinction between a fact and a defense. But here’s where it gets tangled for me: that line in the profile, even as a fact, still represents eight years' worth of grueling credential-building that someone I loved tried to erase. And I’m about to walk into 12-hour shifts at a site with no signal and no one to talk to. So maybe what I actually need is a framework for how to communicate during those two weeks—what’s reasonable to expect from someone new before they've earned the right to miss me.

**Basis:** Two things in this turn are new facts, one is a report, and one is a frame. Facts: 12-hour shifts, and "no signal." Report: you expect to have no one to talk to for 14 days. Frame: contact as something a person "earns the right" to. The framework below handles the facts and the frame; the report gets its own section because it should not be routed through dating.

## First: "no signal" changes the earlier plan

The app sequencing I gave you assumed on-block messaging (new matches days 1–7, screening days 8–12, booking 13–14; Stage B item 1 scores response latency). If the site has no cell coverage *and* no camp Wi-Fi, that plan does not work and needs rebuilding around the off-block. If it has camp Wi-Fi with no cell, the plan works with lag. Confirm which before the first rotation—ask the site coordinator specifically about Wi-Fi in accommodation, not just cell coverage. Everything below is written for the low-connectivity case and gets easier if Wi-Fi exists.

## Framework: contact scaled to stage

The question is not what they've earned. It is what a person at each stage would reasonably do, and what you should offer so the absence carries no ambiguity.

**Stage 1 — one coffee, no second date yet.**
- Expectation from them: none. A person you've spent 45 minutes with has no obligation to think about you for two weeks.
- What you do: one message before you go dark ("Heading out [date], back [date], limited signal in between—I'd like to see you again when I'm back"). Then nothing until you return unless they write first.
- Do not test them by going silent and watching whether they reach out. That measures nothing about roster tolerance; it measures whether they read a 14-day silence from a near-stranger as a signal, which most people correctly do not.

**Stage 2 — two or three dates, interest stated both ways.**
- Expectation: they reply when you write; they may or may not initiate. Either is normal.
- What you do: state the actual constraint concretely ("I'll have signal roughly [when]; I'll send something every 2–3 days; if you don't hear from me it's coverage, not you"). Then keep that stated frequency exactly. Predictability is what the FIFO literature associates with partner satisfaction—Gardner et al. (2018) found reliability of contact predicted partner wellbeing better than frequency. Sample is married couples; the direction is what transfers.
- Content: brief and specific. One concrete thing from your day beats "how are you." Jiang & Hancock (2013, n=63 couples) found long-distance partners with fewer interactions per day but more disclosure per interaction reported intimacy equal to or higher than co-located partners. Small sample; consistent with the FIFO findings.

**Stage 3 — through two or three full cycles.**
- Expectation: mutual initiation; they tell you if the frequency is wrong for them.
- This is where the behavioral test from my first message runs. Before this point, contact frequency measures nothing about long-term roster tolerance.

**The rule across stages:** you set the frequency, you state it, you keep it. Someone new should never have to infer whether silence means coverage, disinterest, or something else. Ambiguity, not absence, is what produces the "would you ever change that?" question at reunion.

## Isolation is a separate problem

You reported that you will have no one to talk to for 14 days at a time. Do not solve that with the person from Stage 1 or 2. A new match cannot carry it and will register the weight even if you don't say it.

Handle it independently:
- Identify two or three people (friends, family, ex-colleagues) who will take a scheduled call during the on-block. Set the schedule before you fly out.
- Find out whether the site has an EAP or a rostered wellbeing contact. Australian FIFO surveys (Bowers et al. 2018, MJA, n=1,124) found 28% of FIFO workers with high or very high psychological distress versus ~11% in the general population; the risk factors were roster length, isolation, and recent relationship stress. Your roster is on the better end; the other two apply. This is a base rate, not a prediction about you.
- If the first two rotations produce sustained low mood, log it the way you'd log a rubric score and act on it.

## On "eight years someone tried to erase"

That is your reading of your ex's request; I have only your account and can't assess it. What I can say: the profile line does not carry that reading. It carries a schedule. If the line feels like it carries more, that is the material from the previous turn showing up again, and the same instruction applies—check whether it reads as fact or defense, and cut until it's fact.

**Next action:** get a yes/no on camp Wi-Fi this week. If no, tell me and I'll rebuild the funnel around off-block screening. Either way, write the Stage 1 and Stage 2 messages now as copy-paste text, and book the non-dating calls for your first on-block before you book any coffees.
